title: Applying standards: bloodborne pathogens, HazCom, and ergonomics
objective: Apply OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens and Hazard Communication standards and safe patient handling principles to realistic health care scenarios.
body:
Health care is one of the most hazardous sectors for workers, and a few OSHA standards appear again and again in practice and on tests.

**Bloodborne Pathogens Standard.** This standard protects workers with reasonably anticipated exposure to blood or **other potentially infectious materials (OPIM)**, with hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV as the main concerns. Employers must have a written **exposure control plan** reviewed at least annually, use **standard precautions** (treating all blood and OPIM as infectious), provide engineering controls such as **sharps with engineered injury protection** and puncture-resistant sharps containers, and offer the hepatitis B vaccine at no cost to exposed employees. Contaminated needles should not be recapped, bent, or broken by hand. After a needlestick, the worker should:
1. Wash the area with soap and water right away
2. Report the exposure to a supervisor immediately
3. Get a confidential medical evaluation promptly, because any post-exposure treatment works best when started quickly

**Hazard Communication Standard (HazCom).** Often called the right-to-know rule, HazCom is aligned with the **Globally Harmonized System (GHS)**. Chemical manufacturers must provide a **Safety Data Sheet (SDS)** with 16 standardized sections, and containers must carry labels with a product identifier, signal word, hazard statements, precautionary statements, pictograms, and supplier information. There are only two signal words: **Danger** for more severe hazards and **Warning** for less severe ones. Pictograms appear as a black symbol inside a red diamond border; for example, the flame means flammable, the skull and crossbones means acute toxicity, and the exclamation mark means irritant or lesser hazards. Employers must keep SDSs readily accessible and train workers on them.

**Safe patient handling.** Manual lifting of patients is a leading cause of back injuries among nurses and aides. NIOSH research suggests that manually lifting more than about 35 pounds of a patient's weight is unsafe in most situations, so facilities increasingly use mechanical lifts, slide sheets, and lift teams. Good body mechanics still matter: keep a wide base of support, hold the load close, bend at the hips and knees, and pivot with the feet instead of twisting the spine.

**Other recurring hazards** include workplace violence (health care workers face high rates of assault), latex allergy, and slips on wet floors. Each is managed with the same hierarchy-of-controls thinking from foundational safety.

The most common mistake students make is thinking good body mechanics alone make patient lifting safe. Body mechanics reduce risk, but for heavy or dependent patients the correct answer is an engineering control such as a mechanical lift, not simply lifting with the legs.
examples: A phlebotomist uses a needle with a built-in safety shield and drops it directly into a sharps container without recapping it.
A custodian checks the SDS for a new floor stripper and finds in Section 8 that splash goggles and gloves are required.

questions.stem: An aide is stuck by a used needle while emptying a trash bag. What should she do first?
choices: Wash the site with soap and water
Wait to see if symptoms develop before reporting
Squeeze the wound and apply bleach
Finish the shift and report the next day
questions.explanation: Immediate washing with soap and water is the first step, followed by prompt reporting and evaluation. Delaying the report is the main error, because post-exposure treatment is most effective when started quickly.

questions.stem: A container label shows the signal word 'Danger.' What does this tell a worker compared with 'Warning'?
choices: The chemical is flammable
The hazard is more severe
The chemical is only harmful if swallowed
The container is under pressure
questions.explanation: Under GHS, 'Danger' marks more severe hazards and 'Warning' less severe ones. The signal word does not identify a specific hazard type such as flammability; pictograms do that.

questions.stem: Under the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, how must the hepatitis B vaccine be offered to exposed employees?
choices: Only after an exposure incident
At the employee's own expense
At no cost to the employee
Only to employees who request it in writing after one year
questions.explanation: Employers must offer the vaccine free of charge to employees with occupational exposure. Offering it only after an exposure would miss the point of preventing infection beforehand.

questions.stem: A nursing assistant needs to move a 220-pound patient who cannot bear weight from bed to chair. Which approach best reflects current safe patient handling practice?
choices: Lift with the legs using good body mechanics
Ask one coworker to help and lift together
Use a mechanical lift according to facility protocol
Have the patient hold the aide's neck during the transfer
questions.explanation: A mechanical lift removes the heavy load from workers, which is an engineering control. Two-person manual lifting is the tempting distractor, but it still exceeds safe lifting limits for a dependent patient.

questions.stem: Where would a worker find the recommended PPE for handling a chemical?
choices: On the OSHA 300 log
In the Safety Data Sheet
On the exposure control plan only
On the OSHA poster
questions.explanation: The SDS lists exposure controls and personal protection. The exposure control plan addresses bloodborne pathogens, not chemical PPE details.

questions.stem: A student sees a pictogram with a skull and crossbones. What hazard does it indicate?
choices: Acute toxicity
Corrosive to skin
Environmental hazard
Gas under pressure
questions.explanation: The skull and crossbones signals acute toxicity that can be fatal or toxic. Corrosion is shown by a different pictogram depicting liquid eating into a hand and a surface.

questions.stem: A clinic manager asks how often the written exposure control plan must be reviewed and updated. What is correct?
choices: Every five years
Only after an OSHA inspection
At least annually
Only when a new employee is hired
questions.explanation: OSHA requires review at least annually and whenever procedures change. Waiting for an inspection would leave the plan outdated and out of compliance.

questions.stem: Which practice violates the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard?
choices: Placing a used needle in a puncture-resistant sharps container
Recapping a used needle with two hands before disposal
Wearing gloves when drawing blood
Treating all blood as potentially infectious
questions.explanation: Two-handed recapping is prohibited because it causes needlesticks. The other choices are required or recommended practices.

flashcards.definition: Other potentially infectious materials, such as certain body fluids and tissues, covered along with blood by the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard.
An employer's written plan to eliminate or minimize bloodborne pathogen exposure, reviewed at least annually.
A 16-section document describing a chemical's hazards, safe handling, PPE, and emergency measures.
The GHS label word showing hazard severity: Danger for more severe, Warning for less severe.
Treating all blood and potentially infectious materials as if they are infectious.
